goals: Explain why carbon forms covalent bonds by sharing electrons
Draw electron-dot structures of H2, O2, N2, CH4 and CO2

slides.heading: Carbon and its Compounds
slides.body_md: Part 1 — why carbon **shares** electrons, how covalent bonds explain the properties of carbon compounds, and why carbon can form millions of compounds, starting with **hydrocarbons**.

visual.alt: Methane burns in oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water
visual.caption: Methane is the main gas in CNG and in biogas.

slides.narration: Namaste! The LPG in your kitchen, the petrol in a scooter, the cotton of your shirt, the sugar in your chai and even the DNA in your cells are all carbon compounds. Scientists know of many millions of them, far more than for any other element. In this part we find out how carbon atoms bond, why that bonding gives carbon compounds their properties, and how carbon builds chains, branches and rings.

slides.heading: Carbon's problem: four outer electrons
slides.body_md: Carbon (atomic number 6) has electronic configuration **2, 4**. To reach a stable octet it would have to gain or lose four electrons — both are very difficult. So carbon **shares** electrons, forming **covalent bonds**.

rows: Six protons cannot hold ten electrons firmly
A very large amount of energy would be needed

visual.alt: Table of carbon’s three options for reaching an octet: gaining or losing four electrons is unfavourable, so carbon shares electrons

slides.narration: Carbon has four electrons in its outer shell, exactly halfway to eight. Gaining four would mean six protons trying to hold ten electrons, which they cannot do well. Losing four would need a huge amount of energy. So carbon takes the third route: it shares its electrons with other atoms. A shared pair of electrons between two atoms is a covalent bond, and carbon forms four of them.

slides.heading: Sharing electrons: hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen
slides.body_md: One shared pair makes a **single bond**, two pairs a **double bond**, three pairs a **triple bond**. Non-metals such as hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen form molecules this way.

slides.narration: Two hydrogen atoms each have one electron. By sharing them, both get a full first shell of two. Oxygen atoms have six outer electrons each, so they share two pairs, a double bond, to reach eight. Nitrogen atoms have five each and share three pairs, a triple bond. That triple bond is very strong, which is why the nitrogen of the air is so unreactive. Count the electrons around each atom on screen to check.

slides.heading: Methane and carbon dioxide
slides.body_md: In **methane**, carbon shares one pair with each of four hydrogen atoms. In **carbon dioxide**, carbon shares two pairs with each oxygen atom.

slides.narration: Look at methane first. Carbon brings four electrons, each hydrogen brings one, and each pair is shared. Now carbon has eight around it and every hydrogen has two. In carbon dioxide, carbon forms a double bond with each oxygen. Count around carbon: four shared pairs, eight electrons. Count around each oxygen: two shared pairs plus two lone pairs, eight again. Both molecules satisfy everyone.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: electron-dot structure of ammonia
slides.body_md: Draw the electron-dot structure of ammonia, $\ce{NH3}$ (N = 7, H = 1).
bullets: Step 1 — outer electrons: N has 5 (2, 5); each H has 1.
Step 2 — nitrogen needs 3 more, each hydrogen needs 1 more: so N forms **3 single bonds**, one with each H.
Step 3 — draw one shared pair between N and each H.
Step 4 — nitrogen's remaining 2 electrons stay as a **lone pair**.
Check — around N: 3 shared pairs + 1 lone pair = 8 electrons; around each H: 2 electrons.

visual.alt: Worked table for ammonia: nitrogen with five outer electrons forms three single bonds to hydrogen and keeps one lone pair

slides.narration: Here is a routine that works for any small molecule. First, write the outer electrons of each atom. Next, work out how many each still needs. Nitrogen needs three, so it shares one pair with each of three hydrogens. The two electrons nitrogen did not share stay together as a lone pair. Finally, count: eight around nitrogen and two around each hydrogen. If every atom is satisfied, your structure is right.

slides.heading: Properties of covalent compounds
slides.body_md: Bonds **inside** a covalent molecule are strong, but the forces **between** molecules are weak.

rows: Weak forces between molecules are easily overcome
Many are gases or liquids at room temperature
They are made of molecules, not ions, so no charged particles move
Often dissolve in kerosene or petrol rather than water

visual.alt: Table of properties of covalent compounds with reasons: low melting and boiling points, poor conductivity, solubility in organic solvents

slides.narration: Covalent compounds behave very differently from salts. A candle melts on a warm day and petrol evaporates quickly, because the forces between their molecules are weak, even though the bonds inside each molecule are strong. They also do not conduct electricity: there are no ions, only neutral molecules. Compare common salt, which melts only at about eight hundred degrees Celsius and conducts when molten.

slides.heading: Diamond and graphite: two forms of carbon
slides.body_md: Different arrangements of carbon atoms give **allotropes**. In **diamond** each carbon bonds to four others in a rigid network: the hardest natural substance. In **graphite** each carbon bonds to three others in flat **hexagonal layers**: smooth, slippery and a **good conductor**. **Fullerenes** such as $\ce{C60}$ are a third form.

slides.narration: Diamond and pencil lead are both pure carbon. The difference is the arrangement. In diamond, every carbon atom is locked to four neighbours in all directions, making it extremely hard; it is used in drills and glass cutters. In graphite, each carbon bonds to three neighbours in flat sheets that slide over one another, which is why pencil lead feels slippery. Graphite also conducts electricity, so it is used for electrodes.

slides.heading: Why carbon forms so many compounds
slides.body_md: **Catenation**: carbon atoms link to one another to form long chains, branches and rings. **Tetravalency**: each carbon forms four bonds, with carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine and more. Carbon bonds are **strong** because carbon atoms are small.

nodes.label: Catenation: carbon–carbon chains, branches and rings

visual.alt: Flow: catenation, tetravalency and strong bonds together lead to millions of carbon compounds

slides.narration: Three features make carbon special. First, catenation: carbon atoms join to other carbon atoms to make chains hundreds of atoms long, as well as branches and rings. Silicon can only manage chains of about seven or eight atoms, and those are quite reactive. Second, tetravalency: four bonds per atom, to many different elements. Third, carbon is small, so its bonds are short and strong. Together they give millions of stable compounds.

slides.heading: Saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons
slides.body_md: **Hydrocarbons** contain only carbon and hydrogen. **Saturated** ones (alkanes) have only single bonds. **Unsaturated** ones have a double bond (alkenes) or a triple bond (alkynes) between carbon atoms.

visual.alt: Table comparing alkanes, alkenes and alkynes by bond type, general formula and first member

slides.narration: Hydrocarbons are the simplest carbon compounds. If every carbon–carbon bond is single, each carbon holds as many hydrogens as it possibly can, so we call the compound saturated, like a sponge full of water. These are alkanes. If two carbons share a double bond, there is room for fewer hydrogens: an alkene. A triple bond gives an alkyne. Notice the general formulas: each extra bond between carbons removes two hydrogens.

slides.heading: Ethane, ethene and ethyne
slides.body_md: All three have two carbon atoms. Each carbon still forms **four bonds** in total.

slides.narration: Here are the three two-carbon hydrocarbons. In ethane the carbons share one pair, and each carbon carries three hydrogens. In ethene they share two pairs, so each carbon carries only two hydrogens. In ethyne they share three pairs, leaving room for one hydrogen each. Ethyne, also called acetylene, burns with a very hot flame and is used in welding. Always check that each carbon has exactly four lines.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: electron-dot structure of ethene
slides.body_md: Draw the electron-dot structure of ethene, $\ce{C2H4}$.
bullets: Step 1 — join the two carbons with a single pair and give each carbon two hydrogens: each carbon now has only 3 shared pairs (6 electrons).
Step 2 — each carbon still needs one more pair, so the carbons share a **second pair**: a double bond.
Step 3 — total shared pairs: 4 C–H pairs + 2 C–C pairs = **6 shared pairs** (12 electrons).
Check — each carbon: 4 shared pairs = 8 electrons; each hydrogen: 2 electrons; no lone pairs.

visual.alt: Worked table for ethene: four carbon–hydrogen bonds and one carbon–carbon double bond, six shared pairs in total

slides.narration: Start with the skeleton: two carbons joined, two hydrogens on each. Now count around one carbon: two pairs to hydrogens and one pair to the other carbon, only six electrons. Both carbons are short of one pair, so they share a second pair between them. That is the double bond. Count again: eight around each carbon, two around each hydrogen, and six shared pairs altogether.

slides.body_md: Carbon atoms can link in a **straight chain**, a **branched chain** or a **ring**. Cyclohexane, $\ce{C6H12}$, is a saturated ring; benzene, $\ce{C6H6}$, is a ring with alternating single and double bonds.

visual.caption: Hydrogen atoms are left out so that the carbon skeleton is clear. The two four-carbon structures have the same formula, C₄H₁₀.

slides.narration: Carbon skeletons come in three shapes. In a straight chain, the carbons are joined one after another. In a branched chain, one carbon sticks out sideways. In a ring, the chain closes on itself. Cyclohexane is a six-carbon ring with only single bonds. Benzene is also a six-carbon ring, but with alternating single and double bonds. Hydrogen atoms are left out of these drawings to keep the skeleton clear.

slides.heading: Structural isomers
slides.body_md: Compounds with the **same molecular formula** but **different structures** are **structural isomers**. Butane, $\ce{C4H10}$, has two: a straight chain and a branched chain. They have different properties.

rows: Chain of 3 carbons with a branch

visual.alt: Table comparing the two structural isomers of butane: straight-chain butane boils at about 273 K and branched isobutane at about 261 K
visual.caption: Both isomers are found in the LPG used in Indian kitchens.

slides.narration: The gas in an LPG cylinder is mostly butane and propane. Butane comes in two versions with exactly the same formula, four carbons and ten hydrogens, but different shapes. One is a straight chain and the other is branched. Because their shapes differ, so do their properties: the branched isomer boils at a lower temperature. Same formula, different structure: that is what we mean by structural isomers.

slides.body_md: What is the molecular formula of cyclohexane?
slides.narration: Quick check. Draw a ring of six carbons in your notebook. Each carbon is bonded to two other carbons, so how many hydrogens can each one hold? Multiply and choose.

slides.heading: The first six alkanes
slides.body_md: Learn the names of the first six saturated hydrocarbons; they are the roots for naming every other compound.

visual.alt: Table of the first six alkanes with number of carbon atoms, name, formula and an everyday source

slides.narration: Here are six names to learn by heart: methane, ethane, propane, butane, pentane and hexane, for one to six carbon atoms. A memory aid: Mummy Eats Pakoras But Prefers Halwa. Each formula fits the alkane pattern: twice as many hydrogens as carbons, plus two. These roots, meth, eth, prop, but, pent and hex, will name every compound in Part 2.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: Carbon (2, 4) shares electrons to form four covalent bonds.
Single, double and triple bonds share one, two and three pairs: $\ce{H2}$, $\ce{O2}$, $\ce{N2}$; $\ce{CH4}$ and $\ce{CO2}$.
Covalent compounds: low melting and boiling points, poor conductors (no ions).
Diamond (4 bonds per C, hardest) and graphite (3 bonds per C, layers, conducts) are allotropes.
Catenation + tetravalency → millions of compounds: chains, branches, rings; saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons; isomers.

rows: Carbon bonding to carbon in chains and rings

visual.alt: Summary table of key terms from Part 1 with meanings and examples

slides.narration: Let us wrap up Part 1. Carbon cannot easily gain or lose four electrons, so it shares them in covalent bonds. Single, double and triple bonds share one, two and three pairs. Weak forces between molecules give covalent compounds low melting points, and the lack of ions makes them poor conductors. Catenation and tetravalency let carbon build chains, branches and rings, saturated and unsaturated, and even isomers.

slides.heading: Exam tips: covalent bonding and hydrocarbons
bullets: Electron-dot structures: show **only outer electrons**, use dots and crosses for different atoms, and check 8 around C, N, O and 2 around H.
Count bonds carefully: $\ce{N2}$ has a triple bond; $\ce{O2}$ a double bond; $\ce{CO2}$ two double bonds.
"Why don't covalent compounds conduct?" — no ions (and no free electrons).
Graphite conducts because each carbon bonds to only three others; diamond does not.
Alkanes $C_nH_{2n+2}$, alkenes $C_nH_{2n}$, alkynes $C_nH_{2n-2}$; cyclohexane is $\ce{C6H12}$ even though it is saturated.
A typical 3-mark answer: correct structure (1–2) + reason or property (1).
slides.narration: Here is how to score full marks. In electron-dot structures, show only the outer electrons and count to eight around every carbon, nitrogen and oxygen, and two around hydrogen. Remember the triple bond in nitrogen. Explain poor conductivity by saying there are no ions. Know why graphite conducts. Learn the three general formulas, and watch out for cyclohexane: it is saturated but does not fit the alkane formula, because it is a ring.

decks.title: Carbon and its Compounds — Part 2: Functional groups, naming and reactions
goals: Identify halogen, alcohol, aldehyde, ketone and carboxylic acid functional groups
State the features of a homologous series
Name carbon compounds with up to six carbon atoms
Write equations for combustion, oxidation of alcohols, hydrogenation and substitution by chlorine

slides.heading: Families, names and reactions
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how a **functional group** decides a compound's family, how families form **homologous series**, how to **name** compounds, and four kinds of **reactions**.

edges.label: same group, chains of different length

visual.alt: Flow from a hydrocarbon skeleton to a functional group, then to a homologous series and a systematic name

slides.narration: Welcome back. A carbon skeleton on its own is just a hydrocarbon. Swap one hydrogen for a small group of atoms, such as oxygen and hydrogen together, and the compound gains a whole new personality. These groups are called functional groups. In this part you will learn to spot them, see how they make families of compounds, name compounds like a chemist, and write four important kinds of reactions.

slides.heading: Functional groups
slides.body_md: A **functional group** is an atom or group of atoms (a **heteroatom** such as O, N or Cl) that gives a compound its characteristic properties, whatever the length of the carbon chain.

visual.alt: Table of five functional groups with formula, family and an example of each

slides.narration: Think of a functional group as a badge that decides how a compound behaves. The hydroxyl group, oxygen bonded to hydrogen, makes an alcohol. The carboxyl group makes an acid, like the acetic acid in vinegar. Aldehydes and ketones both contain carbon double-bonded to oxygen: in an aldehyde it sits at the end of the chain, in a ketone it sits in the middle. Halogens such as chlorine make haloalkanes.

slides.heading: Homologous series
slides.body_md: A **homologous series** is a family of compounds with the **same functional group**, in which successive members differ by a $\ce{CH2}$ unit (14 u).
bullets: Same general formula, e.g. alkanes $C_nH_{2n+2}$.
**Similar chemical properties** (same functional group).
**Gradation** in physical properties: melting point, boiling point and density rise with molecular mass.

visual.alt: Boiling points of the first six alkanes rise steadily with chain length: methane about 112 K, ethane 185 K, propane 231 K, butane 273 K, pentane 309 K, hexane 342 K
visual.caption: Room temperature is about 298 K: the first four alkanes are gases, pentane and hexane are liquids.

slides.narration: Members of a homologous series are like siblings who keep growing: each one is one carbon and two hydrogens longer than the one before, adding fourteen units of mass. Because they share the same functional group, they react in similar ways. But their physical properties change gradually. Look at the graph: boiling points climb steadily from methane to hexane. The same happens in alcohols: methanol boils at about three hundred and thirty eight kelvin, butanol at about three hundred and ninety one.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: next members of a series
slides.body_md: The first member of the alcohol series is methanol, $\ce{CH3OH}$. Write the formulas of the next two members and find the difference in molecular mass between methanol and the third member. (C = 12 u, H = 1 u, O = 16 u)
bullets: Step 1 — add one $\ce{CH2}$ each time: ethanol $\ce{C2H5OH}$, then propanol $\ce{C3H7OH}$.
Step 2 — molecular masses: methanol $12 + 4 + 16 = 32$ u; propanol $36 + 8 + 16 = 60$ u.
Step 3 — difference = $60 - 32 = 28$ u.
Check — two $\ce{CH2}$ steps: $2 \times 14 = 28$ u.

visual.alt: Worked table of the first three alcohols with formulas and molecular masses 32, 46 and 60 u, each differing by 14 u

slides.narration: Building a series is like adding one bead at a time. Methanol has one carbon; add a carbon and two hydrogens and you get ethanol; add another and you get propanol. Now the masses: methanol is thirty two, ethanol forty six, propanol sixty. Each step adds fourteen. So the difference between the first and third members is twenty eight. Always check with the shortcut: number of steps times fourteen.

slides.heading: Quick check: what stays the same?
slides.body_md: Which statement is NOT true for members of a homologous series?
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember the three features: same functional group, a constant difference in formula, and a steady change in one kind of property. Find the statement that breaks the pattern.

slides.heading: Naming carbon compounds in three steps
slides.body_md: Use the **root** for the number of carbons (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-), then show the functional group as a **prefix** or **suffix**. Drop the final "e" of the root before a suffix that begins with a vowel.

nodes.label: Count the carbons, including the one in the functional group
Choose the root: meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex
Add prefix or suffix: chloro-, bromo-, -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid, -ene, -yne

visual.alt: Flow for naming: count carbons, choose the root, then add the prefix or suffix for the functional group

slides.narration: Naming follows a recipe. Step one: count every carbon atom, including the carbon inside groups like the aldehyde or acid group. Step two: pick the root word. Step three: add the label for the functional group. Halogens go in front, as chloro or bromo. Alcohols end in ol, aldehydes in al, ketones in one, and acids in oic acid. Double and triple bonds change ane to ene and yne.

slides.heading: Names in action
slides.body_md: Each name tells you the chain length and the family.

visual.alt: Table of six structures with their carbon count, functional group and systematic name

slides.narration: Let us read a few names. Three carbons with a chlorine at the end is chloropropane. Three carbons ending in an aldehyde group is propanal: notice we count the carbon of the aldehyde group. Put the carbon and oxygen in the middle of three carbons, and it becomes propanone, the nail-polish remover. Four carbons ending in an acid group is butanoic acid, which gives rancid butter its smell.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: naming two compounds
slides.body_md: Name (a) $\ce{CH3CH2CH2CH2CHO}$ and (b) $\ce{CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2Br}$.
bullets: Step 1 (a) — count carbons: 4 in the chain + 1 in –CHO = **5**, root **pent**.
Step 2 (a) — –CHO is an aldehyde: suffix **-al**. Pentane → drop "e" → **pentanal**.
Step 3 (b) — 5 carbons, root **pent**; the halogen is bromine: prefix **bromo-** → **bromopentane**.
Check — both names begin with the chain length and show the family.

visual.alt: Worked table naming a five-carbon aldehyde as pentanal and a five-carbon bromo compound as bromopentane

slides.narration: The commonest mistake with aldehydes is forgetting to count the carbon inside the aldehyde group. In the first compound, four carbons sit in the chain and one more sits in the aldehyde group, five in all, so the root is pent and the name is pentanal. The second compound has five carbons and a bromine atom, so it is bromopentane. Halogens always go in front as a prefix.

slides.heading: Quick check: name it
slides.body_md: What is the name of $\ce{CH3CH2CH2Cl}$?
slides.narration: Quick check. Count the carbon atoms, decide whether the chlorine is shown as a prefix or a suffix, and pick the matching name.

slides.heading: Combustion: carbon compounds as fuels
slides.body_md: Carbon compounds burn in oxygen to give **carbon dioxide and water**, releasing **heat and light**.

visual.alt: Methane burns completely to carbon dioxide and water
visual.caption: Plenty of heat and light are released: that is why carbon compounds are used as fuels.

slides.narration: Most fuels we use are carbon compounds: LPG, petrol, diesel, kerosene, CNG, wood and coal. When they burn completely in enough oxygen, the carbon becomes carbon dioxide and the hydrogen becomes water, and a lot of heat is released. Methane in a biogas plant and ethanol in a spirit lamp both burn this way. That heat cooks our food and runs our vehicles.

slides.heading: Clean flame or sooty flame?
slides.body_md: **Saturated** hydrocarbons usually burn with a **clean blue flame**. **Unsaturated** compounds burn with a **yellow, sooty flame**. A blue flame can turn yellow and sooty if the **air supply is limited** (incomplete combustion).

visual.caption: Saturated fuels such as LPG burn with a blue flame; unsaturated compounds and poorly aerated burners give a sooty yellow flame.

slides.narration: Look at a gas stove: LPG, a saturated fuel, burns with a clean blue flame. Now light a piece of camphor or a kerosene wick: a yellow flame with black smoke. If the bottom of your cooking pots turns black, the burner holes are probably blocked, so not enough air reaches the gas and burning is incomplete. Cleaning the burner restores the blue flame and saves fuel. Incomplete burning can also make poisonous carbon monoxide.

slides.heading: Oxidation of alcohols
slides.body_md: **Oxidising agents** such as **alkaline potassium permanganate** or **acidified potassium dichromate** add oxygen to alcohols, turning them into **carboxylic acids**. Combustion is also oxidation.

visual.alt: Ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid by an oxidising agent
visual.caption: The pink colour of alkaline potassium permanganate disappears as it is used up.

slides.narration: Add a few drops of pink alkaline potassium permanganate to warm ethanol, one drop at a time. At first the pink colour disappears, because the permanganate is used up as it oxidises the ethanol. Once all the ethanol has reacted, extra drops stay pink. The product is ethanoic acid. In equations we often show the oxygen supplied by the oxidising agent as O in square brackets.

slides.heading: Addition: hydrogenating vegetable oils
slides.body_md: Unsaturated compounds **add hydrogen** across a double bond in the presence of a **catalyst** such as **nickel** or **palladium**. This turns vegetable oils into solid **vanaspati**.

visual.alt: Ethene adds hydrogen in the presence of nickel to form ethane

slides.narration: Vegetable oils contain long chains with double bonds. When hydrogen gas is bubbled through hot oil with a nickel catalyst, hydrogen adds across the double bonds and the liquid oil becomes a solid fat, like vanaspati ghee. This is an addition reaction: two molecules join to make one, with nothing left over. Doctors advise using oils with unsaturated fats more often than saturated fats, which are linked to heart disease.

slides.heading: Substitution: alkanes in sunlight
slides.body_md: Saturated hydrocarbons are fairly unreactive, but in **sunlight** chlorine **replaces** hydrogen atoms one by one: a **substitution** reaction.

visual.alt: Methane and chlorine in sunlight give chloromethane and hydrogen chloride

slides.narration: Alkanes ignore most chemicals, but mix methane with chlorine in sunlight and something happens. A chlorine atom takes the place of a hydrogen atom, making chloromethane and hydrogen chloride. With more chlorine, a second, third and fourth hydrogen can be replaced in turn. Compare this with addition: in substitution one atom swaps for another and two products form; in addition, atoms simply join and one product forms.

slides.heading: Quick check: what type of reaction?
slides.body_md: Methane reacts with chlorine in sunlight to give chloromethane and hydrogen chloride. What type of reaction is this?
slides.narration: Quick check. Ask yourself: did atoms simply join together, or did one atom take another's place? Then choose.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: classify the reaction
slides.body_md: Classify each reaction as **combustion**, **oxidation**, **addition** or **substitution**, with a reason.
bullets: Step 1 — $\ce{C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O}$: a fuel burning in oxygen → **combustion**.
Step 2 — $\ce{C2H5OH + 2[O] -> CH3COOH + H2O}$: alcohol to acid with an oxidising agent → **oxidation**.
Step 3 — $\ce{C3H6 + H2 ->[Ni] C3H8}$: hydrogen adds across a double bond → **addition**.
Step 4 — $\ce{C2H6 + Cl2 ->[sunlight] C2H5Cl + HCl}$: Cl replaces H → **substitution**.

rows: Cl swaps for H; HCl formed

visual.alt: Worked table classifying four reactions of carbon compounds with the clue for each

slides.narration: Here is a classification routine. If a fuel burns in oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water, it is combustion. If an oxidising agent turns an alcohol into an acid, it is oxidation. If two reactants join into one product across a double bond, it is addition. If one atom swaps for another and a by-product like hydrogen chloride appears, it is substitution. Examiners love asking for the clue as well as the name.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2
bullets: Functional groups: –Cl/–Br, –OH, –CHO, >C=O, –COOH decide the family.
Homologous series: same functional group, differ by $\ce{CH2}$ (14 u), similar chemical properties, gradation in physical properties.
Names: root (meth…hex) + prefix or suffix (chloro-, -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid, -ene, -yne).
Reactions: combustion, oxidation, addition (hydrogenation, Ni catalyst), substitution (chlorine, sunlight).

visual.alt: Summary table of the four reaction types with an example and use of each

slides.narration: Let us wrap up Part 2. Functional groups decide the family, and a family whose members differ by one carbon and two hydrogens is a homologous series. Names combine a root for the number of carbons with a label for the group. Carbon compounds burn as fuels, alcohols are oxidised to acids, unsaturated oils add hydrogen to become vanaspati, and alkanes swap hydrogen for chlorine in sunlight.

slides.heading: Exam tips: functional groups, names and reactions
bullets: When naming aldehydes and acids, **count the carbon in –CHO or –COOH**.
Ketones need at least 3 carbons; propanone is the simplest.
Homologous series: write all three features, and the 14 u difference.
Hydrogenation: mention the **catalyst** (nickel or palladium) and that it is an **addition** reaction.
Substitution needs **sunlight**; write HCl as the second product.
Yellow sooty flame = unsaturated fuel or incomplete combustion; blue flame = complete combustion.
slides.narration: Here is how to score full marks. Count the carbon inside aldehyde and acid groups when naming. Remember that the simplest ketone has three carbons. For a homologous series, give all three features. In hydrogenation, name the catalyst and call it addition. In substitution, mention sunlight and write hydrogen chloride as a product. And link a sooty flame to unsaturated fuels or to too little air.

decks.title: Carbon and its Compounds — Part 3: Ethanol, ethanoic acid, soaps and detergents
goals: State the properties and uses of ethanol and ethanoic acid
Write equations for the reactions of ethanol and ethanoic acid, including esterification
Explain micelle formation and the cleansing action of soap
Compare the action of soaps and detergents in hard water

slides.heading: Ethanol, ethanoic acid, soaps and detergents
slides.body_md: Part 3 — two carbon compounds you meet every day, **ethanol** and **ethanoic acid**, how they combine into sweet-smelling **esters**, and how **soaps** and **detergents** clean.

visual.alt: Ethanoic acid and ethanol react in the presence of an acid to form the ester ethyl ethanoate and water
visual.caption: Esters give many fruits and perfumes their smell.

slides.narration: Welcome to Part 3. The hand sanitiser on your school desk is mostly ethanol. The vinegar in pickles is a solution of ethanoic acid. Mix the two with a few drops of acid, warm them, and you get a sweet, fruity smell, like pineapple or ripe banana. And the soap you use every morning is made from oils and a base. Let us see how these compounds work.

slides.heading: Ethanol: properties and uses
slides.body_md: **Ethanol**, $\ce{C2H5OH}$, is a colourless liquid that **mixes with water** in all proportions. It is the active ingredient of alcoholic drinks.

rows: Tincture of iodine, cough syrups, tonics
Burns cleanly; made from sugarcane molasses and grain

visual.alt: Table of uses of ethanol with the property behind each

slides.narration: Ethanol is one of the most useful carbon compounds. It dissolves many medicines, so it is used in tincture of iodine and cough syrups. It kills germs, so it is the main ingredient of hand sanitisers. India now blends ethanol made from sugarcane molasses and grain into petrol; the label E twenty means twenty percent ethanol. Drinking alcohol, however, harms the liver and brain and slows reactions, which is why drunk driving is a serious offence.

slides.heading: Ethanol with sodium
slides.body_md: Ethanol reacts with **sodium** to give **sodium ethoxide** and **hydrogen** gas. Like water, the –OH group reacts with sodium.

visual.alt: Sodium reacts with ethanol to form sodium ethoxide and hydrogen gas
visual.caption: The gas burns with a pop: hydrogen.

slides.narration: Drop a small piece of sodium into ethanol, under your teacher's supervision, and you will see bubbles. The gas burns with a pop, so it is hydrogen. The other product is sodium ethoxide. The reaction is much gentler than sodium with water, but it follows the same idea: the hydrogen of the hydroxyl group is replaced by sodium. Testing for alcohols with sodium is one of the classic laboratory reactions.

slides.heading: Ethanol to ethene: dehydration
slides.body_md: Heating ethanol at **443 K** with **excess concentrated sulphuric acid** removes water and gives **ethene**. The acid acts as a **dehydrating agent**.

visual.alt: Ethanol loses water when heated with concentrated sulphuric acid to form ethene

slides.narration: Concentrated sulphuric acid has a strong attraction for water. When ethanol is heated with excess of it, to about four hundred and forty three kelvin, the acid pulls a water molecule out of each ethanol molecule. What remains is ethene, an unsaturated hydrocarbon with a double bond. This is called dehydration, and the acid is the dehydrating agent. Count the atoms: two carbons, six hydrogens and one oxygen on each side.

slides.heading: Alcohol, safety and fuel
slides.body_md: Even small amounts of **methanol** can cause **blindness** or **death**. To stop misuse, industrial ethanol is **denatured** by adding methanol and a **blue dye**. Ethanol is also a cleaner fuel.

nodes.label: Denatured with methanol and blue dye for industry

visual.alt: Flow: molasses or grain is fermented by yeast to ethanol, which is blended into petrol or denatured for industrial use

slides.narration: Ethanol made by fermenting molasses in sugar mills of Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra now powers vehicles as E twenty petrol, cutting oil imports and pollution. But a related compound, methanol, is deadly: even small amounts damage the optic nerve and can kill. Tragedies from illicit liquor are often caused by methanol. To prevent misuse, ethanol for industry is denatured: methanol and a blue dye are added so that nobody drinks it.

slides.heading: Quick check: ethanol and sodium
slides.body_md: Which gas is given off when a small piece of sodium is dropped into ethanol?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about what sodium does to water, and what part of the ethanol molecule behaves like water. Then pick the gas.

slides.heading: Ethanoic acid
slides.body_md: **Ethanoic acid** (acetic acid), $\ce{CH3COOH}$, is a **weak acid**. A 5–8 % solution in water is **vinegar**, used to preserve pickles. Pure ethanoic acid freezes at **290 K**, so in cold weather it looks like ice: **glacial acetic acid**.

visual.alt: Table comparing hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid of the same concentration: ethanoic acid has a higher pH and reacts more slowly, showing it is a weak acid

slides.narration: Ethanoic acid is the sour taste of vinegar, which keeps pickles and chutneys from spoiling. Compare it with hydrochloric acid of the same concentration. Both turn blue litmus red, but universal indicator shows ethanoic acid has a higher pH, and magnesium fizzes more slowly in it. That is because ethanoic acid ionises only partly in water: it is a weak acid. In a cold lab in Shimla, pure ethanoic acid can even freeze into icy crystals.

slides.heading: Esterification: making a sweet smell
slides.body_md: A carboxylic acid and an alcohol react, in the presence of an **acid catalyst**, to form a sweet-smelling **ester** and water. Esters are used in **perfumes** and **flavourings**.

slides.narration: Take one millilitre each of ethanol and glacial ethanoic acid in a test tube, add a few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid, and warm it gently in a water bath for a few minutes. Then pour the mixture into a beaker of water and waft the smell towards you. Instead of the sharp smell of vinegar, you notice a sweet, fruity smell. That is ethyl ethanoate, an ester. Many fruit flavours in ice creams are esters.

slides.heading: Saponification: esters back to acid salts
slides.body_md: An ester heated with an **alkali** such as sodium hydroxide gives back the **alcohol** and the **sodium salt** of the acid. This is **saponification**; the same reaction with oils and fats makes **soap**.

visual.alt: Ethyl ethanoate and sodium hydroxide give ethanol and sodium ethanoate
visual.caption: Saponification means soap-making.

slides.narration: Esters can be broken down again. Heat an ester with sodium hydroxide solution, and you get the alcohol back, together with the sodium salt of the acid. The word saponification comes from a Latin word for soap. When vegetable oils, which are esters of long-chain acids, are boiled with sodium hydroxide, the sodium salts formed are soap. Small soap-making units in many Indian towns use exactly this reaction.

slides.heading: Ethanoic acid with bases and carbonates
slides.body_md: Being an acid, ethanoic acid **neutralises bases** and reacts with **carbonates and hydrogencarbonates** to give a salt, water and **carbon dioxide**.

visual.alt: Ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydrogencarbonate to form sodium ethanoate, water and carbon dioxide
visual.caption: The carbon dioxide turns lime water milky.

slides.narration: Ethanoic acid behaves like any acid you met in Chapter Two. With sodium hydroxide it forms sodium ethanoate and water. With sodium carbonate or baking soda it fizzes, giving off carbon dioxide that turns lime water milky. Pour a little vinegar on baking soda in your kitchen and you will see the same fizz. This fizz is also the simplest way to tell ethanoic acid from ethanol.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: ethanol or ethanoic acid?
slides.body_md: Two unlabelled bottles hold colourless liquids: one is ethanol, the other dilute ethanoic acid. Plan tests to tell them apart.
bullets: Step 1 — **litmus**: ethanoic acid turns blue litmus red; ethanol has no effect.
Step 2 — **sodium hydrogencarbonate**: ethanoic acid fizzes and the gas turns lime water milky; ethanol does not fizz.
Step 3 — **smell** (wafted carefully): vinegar smell for the acid.
Check — do not use sodium metal: both liquids give hydrogen with sodium.

rows: Brisk fizz; CO₂ turns lime water milky

visual.alt: Worked table of tests that distinguish ethanoic acid from ethanol: litmus and sodium hydrogencarbonate work, sodium metal does not

slides.narration: Here is how a chemist thinks. Ethanoic acid is an acid, so use acid tests. Blue litmus turns red with the acid but not with ethanol. Baking soda fizzes with the acid but not with ethanol. The best tests give a clear difference. Notice what does not work: sodium metal gives hydrogen with both liquids, because both contain an oxygen–hydrogen group. An examiner may give you that as a trap.

slides.heading: Quick check: the right test
slides.body_md: Which test will distinguish ethanoic acid from ethanol?
slides.narration: Quick check. Choose the test that gives a clearly different result for the two liquids. Remember the trap from the last slide.

slides.heading: A soap molecule
slides.body_md: Soaps are **sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids**. Each molecule has a long **hydrocarbon tail** that dissolves in oil (**hydrophobic**) and an **ionic head** that dissolves in water (**hydrophilic**).

slides.narration: A soap molecule is like a tadpole with two personalities. Its long tail is made of carbon and hydrogen, like oil, so it loves oil and avoids water. Its head is an ionic group, a carboxylate with a sodium ion, so it loves water. This double nature is the whole secret of cleaning. Oil and water normally refuse to mix, but a soap molecule can hold on to both at once.

slides.heading: Micelles: how soap removes oily dirt
slides.body_md: In water, soap molecules form clusters called **micelles**: tails point **inwards** into the oily dirt, ionic heads point **outwards** into the water. The micelles stay suspended as an **emulsion** and are rinsed away.

slides.narration: Most dirt on clothes sticks because of oil and grease, which water alone cannot remove. When you scrub a shirt with soap, the oily tails of soap molecules bury themselves in the grease, while the ionic heads stay in the water. Many molecules surround each oily speck, forming a ball called a micelle. The micelles do not stick together, so rubbing and rinsing carry the dirt away in the water.

slides.body_md: **Hard water** contains **calcium and magnesium salts**. These react with soap to form an insoluble, curdy **scum**, so much soap is wasted and little lather forms.

slides.narration: In many towns, like Jaipur or Bengaluru, tap water is hard. Shake soap with it and, instead of rich lather, you get a white curdy scum that sticks to buckets and bathroom tiles. Calcium and magnesium ions in the water combine with the soap to form insoluble salts. Until all those ions are used up, no lather forms, so a lot of soap is wasted. Detergents do not have this problem.

slides.heading: Detergents
slides.body_md: **Detergents** are generally sodium salts of **sulphonic acids** or ammonium salts with chloride or bromide ions. Their charged ends **do not form insoluble precipitates** with calcium and magnesium ions, so they work well in **hard water**.

rows: Sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid
Sodium salt of a sulphonic acid, or ammonium salt

visual.alt: Table comparing soaps and detergents by chemical nature, behaviour in hard water, cleaning mechanism and uses

slides.narration: Detergents were developed to beat hard water. Their molecules also have a long oily tail and a charged head, so they form micelles and clean the same way soap does. But their heads are different: sulphonate or ammonium groups, which do not form insoluble scum with calcium and magnesium. That is why shampoos and washing powders are detergents. Both soaps and detergents clean by micelles; only their behaviour in hard water differs.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: is this water hard?
slides.body_md: Rohan adds the same amount of soap solution, drop by drop, to 10 mL samples of water and shakes after each drop until lasting lather forms. Interpret his results.
bullets: Step 1 — distilled water needed only 2 drops: no hardness.
Step 2 — well water needed 18 drops and scum formed first: calcium and magnesium ions used up soap.
Step 3 — tap water needed 9 drops: moderately hard.
Step 4 — the more drops needed, the harder the water: well > tap > distilled.
Check — with a detergent, all three would lather after a few drops.

headers: Drops of soap for lasting lather

visual.alt: Worked table: distilled water needed 2 drops of soap, tap water 9 and well water 18 before lasting lather formed, so the well water is hardest

slides.narration: Here is a simple way to compare hardness at home or in the lab. Add soap a drop at a time and count how many drops it takes before lather lasts. Calcium and magnesium ions must be used up first, so harder water needs more drops and shows scum. Rohan's well water needed eighteen drops, so it is the hardest. Repeat the test with a detergent and every sample lathers quickly, which confirms the idea.

slides.heading: Quick check: inside a micelle
slides.body_md: Which statement correctly describes a micelle in water?
slides.narration: Final check. Picture the tadpole-shaped soap molecule: which end loves oil and which end loves water? Then decide which way each end points in a micelle.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 3
bullets: Ethanol: solvent, antiseptic, fuel (E20); reacts with sodium (hydrogen) and with hot concentrated sulphuric acid (ethene). Methanol is poisonous.
Ethanoic acid: weak acid; vinegar; reacts with bases, carbonates and hydrogencarbonates.
Esterification: acid + alcohol → ester + water (acid catalyst); saponification: ester + alkali → alcohol + salt.
Soap molecules form micelles: tails in oil, heads in water. Hard water forms scum with soap; detergents work in hard water.

rows: alcohol + sodium salt of the acid

slides.narration: Let us wrap up the chapter. Ethanol is a solvent, an antiseptic and a fuel, and it reacts with sodium and with hot concentrated sulphuric acid. sections.heading: 1. Covalent bonding in carbon compounds
sections.body_md:
Carbon (2, 4) cannot easily form $\ce{C^4-}$ (six protons cannot hold ten electrons) or $\ce{C^4+}$ (too much energy needed). It **shares** electrons: a shared pair is a **covalent bond**. One, two and three shared pairs make **single, double and triple** bonds: $\ce{H2}$ (single), $\ce{O2}$ (double), $\ce{N2}$ (triple); methane has four C–H single bonds; carbon dioxide has two C=O double bonds.

**Covalent compounds** have low melting and boiling points (weak forces between molecules) and are generally poor conductors of electricity (no ions).

**Allotropes of carbon:** **diamond** — each carbon bonded to four others in a rigid 3-D network; hardest natural substance; non-conductor. **Graphite** — each carbon bonded to three others in hexagonal layers; layers slide; good conductor. **Fullerenes** — e.g. $\ce{C60}$, shaped like a football.

key_terms.definition_md: A bond formed by sharing a pair of electrons between two atoms.
Different physical forms of the same element, e.g. diamond and graphite.
A pair of outer electrons on an atom that is not shared in a bond.

sections.heading: 2. Versatile nature of carbon
sections.body_md:
- **Catenation:** carbon links with other carbon atoms to form long chains, branched chains and rings. (Silicon forms chains of only about 7–8 atoms, and these are reactive.)
- **Tetravalency:** a valency of 4 lets carbon bond with four other atoms — carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine and others.
- Carbon atoms are **small**, so the bonds are **strong** and the compounds stable.
These properties give carbon millions of compounds.

key_terms.definition_md: The ability of an element to form bonds with atoms of the same element, giving chains and rings.
Having a valency of four; carbon forms four covalent bonds.

sections.heading: 3. Hydrocarbons: saturated and unsaturated; chains, branches and rings
sections.body_md:
**Hydrocarbons** contain only carbon and hydrogen.
- **Saturated** (alkanes, single bonds only): $C_nH_{2n+2}$ — methane, ethane, propane, butane, pentane, hexane.
- **Unsaturated**: alkenes (one C=C), $C_nH_{2n}$ — ethene, propene; alkynes (one C≡C), $C_nH_{2n-2}$ — ethyne.
- Carbon skeletons can be **straight**, **branched** or **rings** (cyclohexane $\ce{C6H12}$; benzene $\ce{C6H6}$ with alternating double bonds).
- **Structural isomers**: same molecular formula, different structures, e.g. butane and isobutane ($\ce{C4H10}$).

key_terms.definition_md: A hydrocarbon with only single bonds between carbon atoms (alkane).
A hydrocarbon with at least one double or triple bond between carbon atoms.
Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures.

sections.heading: 4. Functional groups, homologous series and nomenclature
sections.body_md:
**Functional groups** decide the properties: halo (–Cl, –Br), alcohol (–OH), aldehyde (–CHO), ketone (>C=O), carboxylic acid (–COOH).

**Homologous series**: same functional group; successive members differ by $\ce{CH2}$ (**14 u**); same general formula; similar chemical properties; gradation in physical properties (melting and boiling points rise with molecular mass).

**Naming** (up to six carbons): root for the number of carbons (meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex) — count the carbon of –CHO or –COOH — then a prefix or suffix:
- halogen: **chloro-**, **bromo-** (chloropropane);
- alcohol: **-ol** (propanol); aldehyde: **-al** (propanal); ketone: **-one** (propanone);
- carboxylic acid: **-oic acid** (propanoic acid); double bond: **-ene**; triple bond: **-yne**.
Drop the final "e" of the root before a suffix that starts with a vowel.

A series of compounds with the same functional group in which successive members differ by a CH₂ unit.
An atom other than carbon or hydrogen in an organic compound, such as O, N or Cl.

sections.heading: 5. Chemical properties: combustion, oxidation, addition, substitution
sections.body_md:
- **Combustion:** carbon compounds burn in oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water with heat and light. Saturated hydrocarbons usually give a clean **blue** flame; unsaturated ones a **yellow, sooty** flame. Limited air gives incomplete combustion (soot, carbon monoxide).
- **Oxidation:** alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids by **alkaline potassium permanganate** or **acidified potassium dichromate** (oxidising agents).
- **Addition:** unsaturated compounds add hydrogen in the presence of a **nickel or palladium catalyst** (**hydrogenation**), e.g. vegetable oils → vanaspati.
- **Substitution:** in **sunlight**, chlorine replaces hydrogen atoms of alkanes one by one.

key_terms.definition_md: A substance that supplies oxygen to (oxidises) another substance.
Addition of hydrogen to an unsaturated compound in the presence of a catalyst.
A reaction in which one atom or group is replaced by another.
A substance that changes the rate of a reaction without itself being used up.

sections.heading: 6. Ethanol and ethanoic acid
sections.body_md:
**Ethanol** ($\ce{C2H5OH}$): colourless liquid, soluble in water; used in medicines (tincture of iodine, cough syrups), sanitisers, as a solvent and as fuel blended with petrol. Methanol is highly poisonous; **denatured alcohol** contains methanol and a blue dye.
- With sodium: sodium ethoxide + hydrogen.
- With hot concentrated sulphuric acid at 443 K: **dehydration** to ethene.

**Ethanoic acid** ($\ce{CH3COOH}$): weak acid; 5–8 % solution is **vinegar**; pure acid freezes at 290 K (**glacial acetic acid**).
- **Esterification:** acid + alcohol (acid catalyst) → sweet-smelling **ester** + water. Esters are used in perfumes and flavours.
- **Saponification:** ester + sodium hydroxide → alcohol + sodium salt of the acid.
- With bases → salt + water; with carbonates and hydrogencarbonates → salt + water + carbon dioxide.

key_terms.definition_md: A sweet-smelling compound formed when a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol.
The reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol, in the presence of an acid catalyst, to form an ester.
The reaction of an ester with an alkali to form an alcohol and the salt of the acid (soap-making).
Ethanol made unfit for drinking by adding methanol and a dye.

sections.heading: 7. Soaps and detergents
sections.body_md:
**Soaps** are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids. Each molecule has an **ionic, hydrophilic head** and a long **hydrocarbon, hydrophobic tail**.

**Cleansing action:** in water, soap molecules form **micelles** — tails point inwards into the oily dirt, ionic heads point outwards into the water. The micelles form an emulsion and are rinsed away with the dirt.

**Hard water** contains calcium and magnesium salts, which react with soap to form insoluble **scum**; much soap is wasted. **Detergents** (sodium salts of sulphonic acids, or ammonium salts with chloride or bromide ions) do not form insoluble precipitates with these ions, so they lather in hard water. They are used in shampoos and washing powders.

key_terms.definition_md: A cluster of soap molecules with tails inside (around oily dirt) and ionic heads outside in water.
Water-loving: dissolves in water (the ionic head of soap).
Water-repelling: dissolves in oil (the hydrocarbon tail of soap).
An insoluble substance formed when soap reacts with calcium and magnesium ions in hard water.
